newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan firms fear tax rise may choke consumption.
newsitem.headline: Japan firms fear tax rise may choke consumption.

text.p: Japanese firms, particularly retailers, are worried that shoppers will bear the brunt of a rise in Japan's sales tax in April and that higher prices could choke off already feeble consumer spending.

Many firms said on Tuesday they will be unable to cushion consumers -- as some did when the tax was introduced eight years ago -- and will be forced to pass on the bigger tax burden by raising prices and fares.
The tax is due to rise to five percent from three percent on April 1 as part of a drive to curb state borrowing.
Although the revised rate will still be below that of many other industrial nations, it is extremely unpopular and economists say it could jolt Japan's fragile economic recovery.
Retailers are likely to suffer but some manufacturers of consumer durables such as cars and computers remain upbeat about their sales prospects, despite the tax increase.
"Retailers will be hit by the consumption tax rise as it is likely to affect consumer spending," said a spokesman for major department store operator Isetan Co Ltd.

Rival retailer Mitsukoshi Ltd also saw tough times ahead. A Mitsukoshi spokesman said that given the fragile state of the economy, retail sales would take longer to recover than they did when the tax was introduced at the height of the 1980s asset "bubble".
A spokeswoman for leading supermarket chain Daiei Inc was more circumspect. "We don't know yet whether there will be an impact from the tax rise or not," she said.
None of the retailers would make specific comments about the possible impact of the increase -- the first change since the tax was introduced in 1989 -- on their profits.

According to a recent poll by the business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun, about 64 percent of 178 firms surveyed planned to raise wholesale prices or, in the case of retailers, pass the tax rise on to consumers.

Unlike in 1989, many firms will be unable to absorb the extra tax as their health has been hurt by the economy's slow recovery from a post-bubble slump and a rise in materials prices due to the weak yen, the paper said.
As a result, consumers will pay more for books, cigarettes, beer and various other products, including cars and computers.
Railway and air fares will also be raised and Tokyo Disneyland plans to increase its ticket prices.

An analyst at Wako Research Institute of Economics said the tax rise, together with an end to special income tax breaks this year, would push down consumer spending. The analyst predicted department store sales would fall 1.2 percent in 1997/98 and supermarket sales would drop 0.5 percent.
A fall in consumer confidence could be a drag on the recovery, dealing a broader blow to the overall economy.
Consumers would normally rush to the shops in the run-up to a tax rise, but except for some big items such as housing and cars, no such buying spree has so far been detected.
Japan's vehicle production in January posted its biggest year-on-year rise since 1980, boosted by pre-tax rise demand, according to car industry data released on Monday.
But other data on Monday showed that January department store sales rose a scant 0.5 percent from a year earlier and January chain store sales were up only 0.8 percent.
Companies in other sectors also cited worries.

NEC Corp, which has forecast robust PC sales in the fiscal year from April despite the tax rise, said it was concerned about a possible slowdown in overall consumer spending and hoped its business would not suffer.

The Japan Automobile Dealers' Association last week predicted Japan's domestic vehicle demand in calendar 1997 would fall 2.9 percent from last year due to a likely fall-off in consumption after the tax increase.
Some companies, however, remained optimistic.
"In the long term, we expect no big impact on our personal computer sales," a Toshiba Corp spokesman said. Toshiba has also forecast strong PC sales in 1997/98.

Despite the car dealers' pessimistic forecast, Honda Motor Co Ltd said it expected its domestic car sales to grow five percent in calendar 1997 despite the tax rise as it expects its recreational vehicles to remain popular.
Toyota Motor Corp said its 1997 domestic car sales were likely to rise four percent year-on-year.
